title: How to Feel Less Nuts This School Year
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Opening the school year, Stuart argues that managing the inevitable stress of teaching comes down to two disciplines: depressurization of self and simplification of workload. He describes the self as five-part, physical, intellectual, emotional, relational, and volitional, and offers concrete depressurizing actions for each, such as walking, bringing vulnerability into conversation, and taking phone-free weekends. He warns that some common stress-coping habits, like staying up late or fixating on what's wrong, feel good short-term but compound pressure over time. On the workload side, he argues that simplification is a wisdom practice, not just an efficiency hack, and offers the prompt "What would this be like if it were simple?" as a starting habit. The piece functions as a back-to-school framework for sustainable teacher wellbeing rather than a one-time pep talk.
points: Stuart's five-part model of self, physical, intellectual, emotional, relational, and volitional, gives teachers a structured way to diagnose which part of themselves needs depressurizing.
He explicitly flags stress-coping habits that feel good short-term, like staying up late or fixating on grievances, but worsen long-term pressure, a distinction most burnout advice skips.
Simplification of workload is framed as a wisdom discipline, not a productivity trick, tied to the recurring question "What would this be like if it were simple?"
The essay treats depressurization and simplification as complementary, ongoing practices rather than a single fix applied once at the start of the year.
quotes: Instead, we've got to apprentice ourselves to two broad areas of practice: Depressurization of self. Simplification of workload.
Depressurization of self requires a clear eye on what a self actually is. I'm pretty convinced that we're five-part creatures: physical, intellectual, emotional, relational, and volitional.
When you're stressed at work and in life, it's easy to justify staying up late so that you can blow off steam; this feels good for a bit, but it makes waking up the next day more of a drag.
If you're smart and aware of your surroundings, there will always be too much to do. And so you must become more than smart; you must become wise.
Both are part of the journey this year, friend. And all the years after. We won't regret time contemplating, practicing, and playing in these two sandboxes.
